title: Verify the equal-block language of a locally constrained tree-adjoining grammar
statement: Reproduce the nonempty string-language claim in Vijay-Shankar and Joshi, Example 2.5: the locally constrained TAG generates exactly a^n b^n c^n for integers n >= 1 when empty yields are excluded. Transcribe its elementary trees, preserve null-adjoining restrictions at auxiliary roots and feet, prove both language inclusions, and provide derivations for n = 1,...,6. Record separately whether the initial tree admits the empty word. The finite example range is curator chosen.
status_basis: The source presents the equal-block construction with local adjoining constraints. This reproduces that construction, not an unrestricted-TAG claim or an empirical claim about language.
plain_summary: A small formal grammar coordinates three equal blocks of symbols. Making its local restrictions explicit lets readers check strings and derivations without confusing a grammar model with evidence about human language.
assumptions: Use ordered rooted elementary trees and the adjoining operation defined in Section 2.1 of the source.
An auxiliary tree has a distinguished foot with the same nonterminal as its root; local restrictions follow the source's inheritance rules.
Read terminal yields left to right, with distinct symbols a, b, c; record the empty word separately.
The target is weak generative capacity of this grammar, not equivalence of tree structures or psychological models.
scope: One fixed grammar, Example 2.5. The proof concerns all nonempty yields; six short derivations are finite illustrations. Unrestricted label matching is not an acceptable replacement for local adjoining constraints.
target: A faithful grammar transcription, both directions of the language-equality proof, and node-addressed derivation records.
success_criteria: Identify elementary trees, terminal order, foot nodes and every local restriction against the original diagram.
Prove that every completed nonempty derivation yields a^n b^n c^n for some n >= 1.
Prove that every such string has a permitted derivation; a finite sample is insufficient.
Record derivations for n = 1 through 6 with elementary-tree identifiers and adjoining addresses.
State the empty-word convention separately and explain why dropping local restrictions changes the task.
known_results: Example 2.5 supplies a locally constrained TAG for equal ordered blocks.
The preceding source discussion separates this constrained construction from the earlier unrestricted adjoining definition.
The paper distinguishes string-language equality from equality of assigned structural descriptions.
prerequisites: Ordered trees, terminal yields and structural induction.
Adjoining versus substitution and context-free rewriting.
Weak and strong generative capacity; the role of formal grammars in linguistic modeling.
significance: Provides a small benchmark where formal-language semantics matter. It supports later grammar comparisons while separating expressibility from processing and acquisition claims.

requirements.experiment: None for language equality. Processing, acceptability and acquisition claims need independent linguistic or cognitive evidence.
requirements.data: Original elementary-tree diagrams and local-constraint definitions; no corpus or participant data.
requirements.compute: Small symbolic trees and six derivation records; no parser training. Local execution should suffice for this bounded presentation, but nothing has been timed. General grammar induction or exhaustive unrestricted derivation search would be different tasks.
requirements.theoretical_assumptions: The exact adjoining semantics determine the language. Successful formal reproduction would not establish psychological realism.

ai_assessment.rationale: Symbolic assistance fits the inductive target and short examples, but a reviewer should first approve transcription of the scanned grammar and its node restrictions.

clarity.reason: A specific grammar and two language inclusions define success.

decomposability.reason: Transcription, derivation checking and inductive proof are separable.

methods.reason: The source construction and tree induction provide standard methods.

search_or_symbolic.reason: Node-addressed trees allow explicit local checks.

checkability.reason: Short derivations are easy to inspect; language equality still requires proof.

expertise.reason: A formal-language reviewer must confirm TAG conventions and weak versus strong equivalence.

significance.reason: The known result is useful for precise grammar comparisons.

verification_difficulty.reason: A parser may accept sample strings while implementing the wrong constraints.

ai_assessment.uncertainty: No transcription, parser or proof has been executed or reviewed. Scanned notation and differing TAG conventions are the main preparation risks.
ai_assessment.model_scope: No named model evaluated; assumes a tool-using AI that can read mathematical sources, produce inspectable symbolic work and code, and work with a human domain reviewer.

obstacles: Treating a foot as a terminal or allowing adjoining at a prohibited node.
Checking sample yields instead of universal language inclusions.
Confusing string equality with tree-set equality.
Turning a formal example into a claim about human language processing.

steps: Compare every tree and constraint directly with Example 2.5.
Check short derivations with a rule checker separate from the generator.
Review the inductive invariant and construction for arbitrary positive n.
Check the empty-word case and language-equality scope.
validation.human_review_difficulty: Moderate: the small trees are inspectable, but local restrictions and their inheritance require formal-language expertise.
validation.statement_alignment: This reproduces one constrained grammar's nonempty string language. It does not establish the same claim for unrestricted TAGs, classify TAG languages or test a cognitive theory.

known_attempts: The original paper presents the construction and example adjoining steps. No project derivation checker or model trial exists.
unresolved_checks: A human reader should approve the scanned tree transcription and empty-word convention before implementation.
Any comparison with a modern TAG library must specify how it encodes local constraints.

attribution.citation: Vijay-Shankar, K., and Joshi, A. K. (1985), Some Computational Properties of Tree Adjoining Grammars, Proceedings of the 23rd Annual Meeting of the ACL, pages 82-93, Section 2.1 and Example 2.5. DOI: 10.3115/981210.981221.
attribution.curator_credit: Compiled for Theory Research Atlas with AI assistance.

status_search.result: The original construction, local-constraint definitions and archive bibliographic record were inspected. This is an established construction selected for reproduction.
status_search.limitations: This is not an open-problem status claim. An executable transcription still needs human review; empirical adequacy and equivalence to modern grammar libraries were not checked.

epistemic_layers.formal_validity: The proof concerns a precisely interpreted tree-rewriting system and terminal yields.
epistemic_layers.empirical_support: Equal-block expressibility alone supplies no evidence about language distributions, human memory or acquisition.

difficulty.basis: Symbolic assistance fits the inductive target and short examples, but a reviewer should first approve transcription of the scanned grammar and its node restrictions.

correctness.basis: The cited literature supports the calibration target. No project answer has been submitted for review.

novelty.basis: This is a known-result calibration. The chosen bounds and presentation are not claims of scientific novelty.

significance.basis: Provides a small benchmark where formal-language semantics matter. It supports later grammar comparisons while separating expressibility from processing and acquisition claims.
